usage: from the verb 설레다; the sweet nervous feeling before something good
common phrase, e.g. 설렘 가득한 첫날
the verb form; 설레요 = I'm excited/fluttery
the excitement of a first day at work
settings + 의 + 설렘 is a natural pattern
examples: 새 동네로 이사 와서 설렘 반 걱정 반이에요.
Moving to a new neighborhood, I'm half excited, half worried.
반 ... 반 ... = half this, half that
내일 첫 데이트라 설렘 때문에 잠이 안 와요.
Tomorrow's my first date, so I can't sleep from the excitement.
설렘 때문에 = because of the flutter
여행 전날의 그 설렘이 제일 좋아요.
I love that fluttery feeling the night before a trip.
그 설렘 = 'that' excitement, shared feeling
nuance: 설렘 is a warm, positive nervousness, the butterflies before a date, a trip, or a new start, not fear. 20-30s use it constantly online and in speech, often paired with 두근두근. The verb 설레다 conjugates to 설레요 (not 설레여요), a spot people get wrong.
mistakes: Saying 설레여요 instead of 설레요 for the verb
Using 설렘 for general 'excitement' like a thrilling game; that's 신나다, while 설렘 is the soft anticipatory flutter

usage: 여유 covers spare time, money, or mental space
to have no leeway / be stretched thin
peace of mind / mental breathing room
examples: 요즘 일이 많아서 마음의 여유가 없어요.
I've had so much work lately that I have no peace of mind.
마음의 여유 = mental breathing room
주말엔 좀 여유 있게 쉬고 싶어요.
On weekends I want to rest with some breathing room.
여유 있게 = in a relaxed way
돈에 여유가 생기면 여행 가려고요.
When I have some money to spare, I plan to travel.
여유가 생기다 = leeway appears
nuance: 여유 is one of the most useful daily words, it stretches across spare time, spare money, and emotional composure. Koreans value 마음의 여유, so saying 여유가 없어요 is a polite, relatable way to decline plans or explain stress without oversharing. 여유 있게 (relaxed/with margin) is heard everywhere.
mistakes: Forgetting it covers money and time too, not just emotions
Using the adjective as 여유하다; the correct adjective is 여유롭다 or the phrase 여유가 있다

usage: the noun; the verb is 후회하다
feeling that wells up, slightly passive nuance
common phrase, e.g. 후회 없이 살자
examples: 그때 그 집 계약 안 한 게 두고두고 후회예요.
I keep regretting not signing the lease on that place back then.
두고두고 = over and over, lingering
후회 없이 도전해 보고 싶어요.
I want to give it a try without regret.
후회 없이 = regret-free
지금 안 사면 나중에 후회할 것 같아요.
If I don't buy it now, I think I'll regret it later.
후회할 것 같아요 = I think I'll regret
nuance: 후회 is the noun for regret; the verb 후회하다 is already common, but the noun shows up in everyday lines like 후회예요 or 후회가 남아요. The mindset phrase 후회 없이 (without regret) is a popular motto among 20-30s. It points backward at a choice already made, unlike 아쉬움, a softer 'shame it didn't work out.'
mistakes: Confusing it with 아쉬움; 후회 blames your own choice, 아쉬움 is gentler 'too bad'
Saying 후회해요 when you mean the noun; for 'it's a regret' use 후회예요

usage: adjective; a key word for declining things
examples: 비싼 선물은 부담스러우니까 안 주셔도 돼요.
An expensive gift feels like too much, so you don't have to give one.
부담스럽다 = feels burdensome
부담 갖지 말고 편하게 오세요.
Don't feel any pressure, just come comfortably.
부담 갖지 말고 = without feeling pressured
월세가 좀 부담이 돼요.
The monthly rent is a bit of a burden.
부담이 되다 = becomes a burden
nuance: 부담 is essential for navigating Korean social give-and-take. When someone treats you or offers a favor, 부담스러워요 politely signals 'this is too much,' and hosts say 부담 갖지 마세요 to put you at ease. It covers both emotional pressure and financial weight, so 부담이 돼요 works for rent or expectations alike.
mistakes: Translating only as 'burden' and missing the social 'don't trouble yourself' nuance
Using 부담하다 (to bear a cost, formal) when you mean to feel pressure; for feelings use 부담스럽다 or 부담이 되다

usage: active thoughtfulness, putting others at ease
the trait; 배려심이 깊다 = deeply considerate
examples: 임산부 배려석은 비워 두는 게 좋아요.
It's good to keep the priority seats for pregnant women empty.
배려석 = consideration seat (subway)
바쁜데 배려해 주셔서 정말 감사해요.
Thank you so much for being considerate even though you're busy.
배려해 주셔서 = for being considerate
그 친구는 배려심이 깊어서 다들 좋아해요.
That friend is so thoughtful that everyone likes them.
배려심이 깊다 = deeply considerate
nuance: 배려 is consideration shown through action, anticipating others' needs and easing their discomfort, a highly praised quality in Korea. You will literally see it on subway 배려석 (priority seats). Calling someone 배려심이 깊다 is a strong compliment, and 배려해 주셔서 감사해요 is a graceful way to thank someone for their thoughtfulness.
mistakes: Confusing it with 친절 (kindness); 배려 is proactively considering someone's situation, not just being nice
Writing 배려심 when you mean a single act; use 배려 for the act, 배려심 for the trait

usage: the dignity you defend against others
to have strong pride / be stubborn about ego
to be stubborn out of pride
negative nuance, refusing to back down
examples: 사과하기 싫어서 자존심 부리다가 친구랑 멀어졌어요.
I let my pride win and refused to apologize, and drifted apart from my friend.
자존심 부리다 = act out of stubborn pride
그 말 들으니까 자존심이 좀 상했어요.
Hearing that hurt my pride a little.
자존심이 상하다 = pride gets hurt
걔는 자존심이 세서 먼저 연락 안 해요.
They have such strong pride that they never reach out first.
자존심이 세다 = strong ego
nuance: 자존심 is pride in the sense of ego you protect in front of others, easily wounded (자존심이 상하다). It differs from 자존감 (inner self-worth): 자존심 looks outward and can be a flaw when someone 자존심을 부리다, while 자존감 is healthy self-esteem. This distinction comes up constantly in relationship talk among 20-30s.
mistakes: Mixing it up with 자존감; 자존심 is outward ego, 자존감 is inner self-worth
Saying 자존심이 아프다; the correct verb is 자존심이 상하다

examples: 한국어로 말할 때 자신감이 좀 부족해요.
I lack a bit of confidence when speaking Korean.
자신감이 부족하다 = to lack confidence
면접 잘 봐서 자신감이 생겼어요.
The interview went well, so I gained confidence.
자신감이 생기다 = confidence forms
자신감 있게 발표해서 칭찬받았어요.
I presented confidently and got praised.
자신감 있게 = confidently
nuance: 자신감 is confidence in what you can do, a task or skill, and is the everyday word for it. Note the close pair 자신 (self / certainty, as in 자신 있어요 'I'm confident I can') versus 자신감 (the noun 'confidence' as a quality). 자신감 있게 (confidently) is a natural adverbial phrase you'll use describing how you did something.
mistakes: Confusing 자신감 (confidence as a quality) with 자만심 (arrogance/overconfidence)
Using 자신감하다; it is a noun, so pair with 있다/없다/생기다, not 하다

usage: to have a strong sense of responsibility
examples: 그 사람은 책임감이 강해서 일을 믿고 맡길 수 있어요.
That person has a strong sense of responsibility, so you can trust them with work.
믿고 맡기다 = trust and entrust
반려동물을 키우려면 책임감이 필요해요.
If you want to raise a pet, you need a sense of responsibility.
책임감이 필요하다 = responsibility is needed
맡은 일은 책임감 있게 끝낼게요.
I'll finish the work I was given responsibly.
책임감 있게 = responsibly
nuance: 책임감 is the inner trait of taking your duties seriously, prized in Korean workplaces, so 책임감이 강하다 is a top compliment in references and self-introductions. Distinguish it from 책임 (the responsibility itself) and the verb 책임지다 (to take the blame/charge). 20-30s hear it constantly in job interviews and team settings.
mistakes: Confusing 책임감 (the feeling/trait) with 책임 (the duty itself)
Using 책임감하다; pair the noun with 있다/강하다, and use 책임지다 for the verb 'take responsibility'

usage: the capacity to endure and wait
examples: 한국어 공부는 인내심이 정말 필요해요.
Studying Korean really requires patience.
인내심이 필요하다 = patience is needed
애들을 가르치려면 인내심이 많아야 해요.
To teach kids, you need a lot of patience.
인내심이 많다 = to have lots of patience
줄이 너무 길어서 인내심이 바닥났어요.
The line was so long that I ran out of patience.
인내심이 바닥나다 = patience runs dry
nuance: 인내심 is patience as the strength to endure hardship or long waits, slightly more formal and character-focused than the everyday 참다 (to put up with). You'll describe people with 인내심이 강하다/많다 and confess 인내심이 바닥났어요 when fed up. It's a great word for talking about learning, parenting, or long bureaucratic processes in Korea.
mistakes: Using 인내심하다; it's a noun, so use 인내심이 있다/많다 or the verb 참다/견디다
Overusing it in casual venting where 참다 ('I had to put up with it') sounds more natural

examples: 새로 생긴 카페에 호기심이 생겨서 가 봤어요.
I got curious about the new cafe, so I checked it out.
N에 호기심이 생기다 = curiosity arises toward N
저는 호기심이 많아서 뭐든 배우는 걸 좋아해요.
I'm very curious, so I love learning anything.
호기심이 많다 = to have lots of curiosity
호기심에 한국 예능을 봤다가 푹 빠졌어요.
I watched a Korean variety show out of curiosity and got totally hooked.
호기심에 = out of curiosity
nuance: 호기심 is curiosity, the pull to know or try something new, and 호기심이 많다 is a warm compliment about an open, eager personality. The phrase 호기심에 ('out of curiosity, on a whim') is super handy for explaining why you tried something. It pairs with 생기다/들다, not 하다.
mistakes: Saying 호기심하다; use 호기심이 생기다/많다
Confusing it with 관심 (interest/attention); 호기심 is the itch to find out, 관심 is sustained interest or care

usage: the feeling of having done wrong
examples: 다이어트 중인데 야식 먹어서 죄책감이 들어요.
I'm on a diet but ate a late-night snack, so I feel guilty.
죄책감이 들다 = guilt arises
바쁘다고 부모님께 연락 못 해서 죄책감이 좀 있어요.
I feel a bit guilty for not contacting my parents, blaming being busy.
죄책감이 있다 = to carry guilt
거짓말한 게 계속 죄책감으로 남았어요.
The lie I told stayed with me as guilt.
죄책감으로 남다 = to linger as guilt
nuance: 죄책감 is the inward feeling of guilt over something you did, paired most naturally with 들다 (죄책감이 들어요). 20-30s use it lightly and often, even about diet slip-ups or skipping the gym, not only serious wrongs. Don't confuse it with 미안함 (the feeling of being sorry toward a person); 죄책감 is the internal weight on your conscience.
mistakes: Using 죄책감하다; the noun pairs with 들다/느끼다, never 하다
Mixing it with 미안함; 미안함 is 'sorry toward someone,' 죄책감 is the inner guilt itself

usage: the rewarding feeling that effort paid off
examples: 힘들었지만 일을 끝내니까 보람을 느껴요.
It was hard, but finishing the work gives me a sense of fulfillment.
보람을 느끼다 = to feel fulfillment
가르친 학생이 합격해서 정말 보람이 있었어요.
The student I taught passed, so it was truly rewarding.
보람이 있다 = to be worthwhile
오늘은 할 일을 다 해서 보람찬 하루였어요.
I got everything done today, so it was a fulfilling day.
보람찬 하루 = a fulfilling day
nuance: 보람 is the warm payoff feeling when your effort proves worthwhile, the reward of seeing hard work bear fruit. It's a deeply positive word Koreans use about jobs, study, volunteering, or parenting: 보람을 느끼다 (to feel fulfilled) and 보람차다 (rewarding). There's no clean one-word English match, which makes it a satisfying word to add to your everyday vocabulary.
mistakes: Reducing it to 'reward' as in money/prize; 보람 is the inner sense of worthwhileness, not a material payout
Saying 보람하다; use 보람을 느끼다, 보람이 있다, or the adjective 보람차다
